speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The Child Development Co-Savings Act (CDCA) covers a range of benefits in our Marriage and Parenthood (M&P) Package.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Members may recall that we amended the CDCA earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We provided for reimbursement to employers who gave the voluntary week of paternity leave, as well as payment to self-employed men for lost income for the second week of paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We also extended the Child Development Account (CDA) benefits to all eligible children, regardless of their parents' marital status.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We are now amending the Act to introduce further support for parents in caring for and bonding with their children.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The key amendments arise from the enhancements to paternity leave, shared parental leave and adoption leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: These enhancements had been announced at the National Population and Talent Division's Committee of Supply in April this year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Amendments covered in the Bill include amendments to better support mothers on different working arrangements, as well as various amendments to align legislation with policy intent.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This Bill will also amend the CDCA to extend certain leave benefits to unwed parents, a move I announced earlier this year.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I have often said that a father's role in the family is not just to put food on the table, but also to be a good role model to guide his children and mould their values and character in a positive way.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We need to make the conscious choice to be active fathers and we have to cultivate this mindset from the start.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We know that it can be challenging to ensure we have work-life balance, but it is important for us to adopt an active parenting lifestyle.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Our children grow up faster than we realise and they should be our priority now, not later.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We need to make the effort to spend both quantity and quality time with our families when we can.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We need to actively weave in time with family into our schedule.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This was announced by the National Population and Talent Division in April, eight months ahead of time, to give employers sufficient time to prepare.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Both weeks of paternity leave are fully funded by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Couples will now have more flexibility in caring for their newborn and can work out an arrangement that best suits them.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: As with the current one week of Shared Parental Leave, the four weeks will be shared from the mother's maternity leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Shared Parental Leave is also fully funded by the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The amendment is intended to take effect from 1 July 2017 to benefit children born on or after that Page: 51 date.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The combined enhancements to paternity leave and shared parental leave means that a father can take a maximum of eight weeks leave in his baby's first year – comprising two weeks of paid paternity leave, four weeks of paid shared parental leave if his wife so elects to share, six days of paid childcare leave and one week of unpaid infant care leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: These leave enhancements support fathers in experiencing the joys and challenges of parenthood with their wives.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will also be enhancing Adoption Leave, to better support adoptive mothers in caring for their adopted infants.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: This is three times more than the current four weeks.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: Similar to what is provided for maternity leave, the Government will fund the last eight weeks of leave if the adopted child is the first or second child, and the full period of 12 weeks, if the adopted child is the third and subsequent child.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The amendment is intended to apply to adoptive mothers whose formal intent to adopt is on or after 1 July 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: We will also extend maternity leave to unwed mothers, to better support the child's developmental and care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: An unwed person adopting a child would also be eligible for leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: An unwed adoptive mother would be eligible for adoption leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: An unwed man adopting a child would be eligible for paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: The amendments are intended to take effect from 1 January 2017 to benefit children born on or after that date or, in the case of adopted children, the formal intent to adopt is on or after that date.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: While families raise children, instil values in them and nurture them, the Government will continue to complement these efforts by supporting families in their care-giving responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: I encourage all parents to make good use of the leave schemes, to be there for our children and inspire them to do the same for generations to come.

speaker: The Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Tan Chuan-Jin)
text: And my heartfelt thanks, especially, go to the employers who play an important role in supporting families' aspirations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a double celebration for me, both as a Board Member of the Centre for Fathering and as the Government Parliamentary Committee chair for MSF.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Many new parents I know welcome the slew of measures as lending weight to nurture a generation of caring fathers and purging the traditional mindset of the woman as de-facto caregiver for newborns.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, it is still up to the mother whether to decide to share her maternity leave with the father.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Placing the decision in the mother's hands seems like a mixed signal from the Government.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When sharing leave is still left to parents to decide, I am not sure if the take-up rate by fathers will be as rapid as we would like.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As is – I asked a Parliamentary Question on this a few months ago – I note that the number of paternity leave fully taken up by eligible fathers has not been as high as one would expect.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a very significant move and much welcomed by all single mothers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, it took some time coming but I am glad that through the persistent efforts of many Members of Parliament, including those who have retired, the Government has listened and answered our call.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Is MSF supportive of improving housing options to this group, although I know this comes under MND's purview?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Imagine the stress of a pregnant, unwed mother having to deal with basic housing issues on her own, in an undignified manner and unable to feel a sense of security, nor provide a secure environment for her child once he or she is born.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have, for many times in the past, argued for the Government to do less and for the people to do more.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, family life, children and how we define success, not just as parents, not just for our children, we need people, society and individuals to decide whether it is time to reset our highly competitive and academically-focused norms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government can and should put in place Bills like the Child Development Co-Savings (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should continue to give greater support for adoptive mothers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We should most certainly give even much more support for single unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But this is only half the story, and perhaps the easier half of child development.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government cannot stop this ceaseless race, these endless comparisons that parents subject their children to.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: People accuse the Government of setting up high-stress exams; I say, it is neither the Government nor the schools which put the stress on children – it is the parents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Parents blame the PSLE not because it is an exam, but I believe it is because it is a nation-wide exam – one that allows a child in Woodlands to compare himself against another in Chancery Lane, against another in Bishan.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Once we take away the common points of comparison, the argument goes, we no longer have this frenzy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps so, the comparisons can actually stop right now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: When we look, as we should, at child development in a manner that takes into account their health, growth and well-being.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Page: 53 Mdm Speaker, this is what today's Bill was meant to be.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was tabled because we, the legislators, want to encourage young Singaporeans to have babies, to experience the joys of parenthood, to dream and love and cry over the little lives that come out of a happy union.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, we can amend the law to better fulfil these ambitions, but it will take many more tomorrows because we can change the world into a better place for the children of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To do that, we need more than just the law.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to rethink what it means to be a parent, what it means to support our children's development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having children is not an easy decision to make.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a father of two young sons, we wake up every morning feeling tired, dishevelled, covered with spittle and spilt milk.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Amidst all of these is a sense of fulfilment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, while it is not easy for complete families to raise children, it is perhaps even tougher for families that may not have the joy of being complete, through various circumstances, sometimes not of their own doing.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unwed mothers, single fathers make courageous decisions to carry on with the pregnancy with all its attendant risks, pains and for single fathers to also take up the mantle to care for their children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These amendments that are proposed today help them in this journey.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There were people who have pointed out: will these moves encourage a journey away from the traditional model?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But as I have mentioned earlier, it is already not an easy decision for them to make to carry on and have these children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But they have made the difficult decision to carry on to bring the child to term and give the child a fighting chance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I made a point earlier this year during the Budget debate that while all these benefits are useful, they are not the end-all and not the solution.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There are still dramatic changes to the family model, not just in Singapore, but the world over.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The way we live our lives, the way we work, our commitments, our own life expectations, our wants and our needs shape the way we view the family.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, it takes a lot more than laws, as Mr Seah Kian Peng has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a long journey for us to get to this point to have these amendments put in place.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I was younger, I perhaps shared the same views.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You are unencumbered, you are free" – figuratively speaking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But then, perhaps, as fate would have it, love came along.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We got married, settled down and have two wonderful young children.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My eldest son will be three years old very soon, and three years seem to have gone by so quickly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think for all of us in this House, as well as many Singaporeans, we work long hours, and so, there are sometimes a lot of lost opportunities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, I would like to make a case once again for single parents.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They bear the burden of raising their children on their own.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What we have put in place in terms of leave, in terms of Government-paid paternity benefits are useful, but there are still many hindrances in their way.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have also talked a lot about how we can better improve care for children as they grow up.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Government must take the lead in this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we encourage private sector and other employers to do so, perhaps, as the Government, perhaps as a public organisation, we should take the lead in that area.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And I hope that with these amendments, we will move towards a more compassionate, merciful society when it comes to viewing unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have it tough enough and, very often, they come from backgrounds that may not give them the advantages to raise their children single-handedly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They have multiple issues and, if we do not extend a further hand to them, their children may undergo similar circumstances in the future.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But as with children growing up, there is a lot more angst to encounter and a lot of changes to adapt to.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While it is important to continue to promote parenthood within the ambit of marital unions, there is a need to balance it with the recognition that not everyone is so fortunate to be able to sustain a happy marriage, or even obtain it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Economic pressures, relationship problems or errors of judgement may be to blame for marital breakdowns or unwed pregnancies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the most important thing is that children should not be punished for the prejudices and mistakes of adults.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our children will stand most to gain from these equalising moves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, protect the family life of contract workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This percentage will grow, as it is a worldwide trend for developed economies that are restructuring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been predicted that 40% of workers in the US will be independent contractors by 2020.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The profile of short-term contract workers is also changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are getting younger, possessing professional credentials and making the conscious choice to be term contract workers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Page: 55 In the coming years, more of the children benefiting from the enhanced parental leave schemes will see their parents working on term contracts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These parents, and their children, will need better protection of their entitlements for this legislation to be meaningful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers have been known to avoid leave obligations by signing workers on contracts that are shorter than three months and renewing them with breaks in between.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am aware that the tripartite partners have set up new guidelines in June this year where employers are encouraged to treat contracts renewed within a month as continuous and grant leave cumulatively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the longer term, I ask that the Government enact comprehensive laws to better protect term contract workers, as this group is fast becoming a substantial group in the new economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Second, without housing security, parental leave can be meaningless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the biggest issue for divorcees and unwed single parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other than income security and retirement adequacy, housing security is a key foundation stone for our social security system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot stress enough that having a secure roof over one's head is crucial for the proper development of children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Children who grow up in a home that is more or less permanent will experience familiarity and love, while those who need to constantly move around will experience psychological stress due to the uncertainty of residence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some studies have shown that for adults, moving homes can be more stressful than divorce and relationship breakdowns and changing jobs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What more for children who need the certainty in their environment to grow up nurtured and feeling secure?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Ministry must be aware of the housing problems faced by divorcees with custody of young children and unwed single parents with young children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most often, these parents are women, who are thus faced with the dual roles of breadwinner and caretaker.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unwed single parents are not allowed to purchase a subsidised BTO flat because their family unit is not considered an eligible family nucleus.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what can be more nuclear than the parent-child relationship?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Placing unwed single parents in the singles category, who can only buy a flat when they reach the age of 35, is a double whammy for the children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government is depriving the children housing security when they need it most at the very young age at the most crucial phase of their development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only that, by treating their parents as singles, the Government is also refusing to recognise the children and sending a terrible signal of shame to the children, who are innocent and should not suffer the sins of their parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Maybe, to balance against the need to promote parenthood within the ambit of marital unions, the Government could choose to make an exception for a parent, regardless of marital status, to apply for a 2-room BTO flat at any age.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe this will be an acceptable compromise, balanced in favour of the well-being of children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For divorcees with young children, the problem is with hefty mortgage loans linked to the HDB flats that they co-own with their ex-spouses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most will be compelled to sell their flat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many will have to purchase smaller flats and their children will face the psychological stress of dislocation Page: 56 and relocation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Low-income divorcees will find themselves and their children in a terrible situation, as they will not be able to afford to purchase a flat and will not be eligible for a public rental flat until five years later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Economic disruption may become the norm, but we should keep disruption to family life minimal.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The problem may well be that the HDB flat has long been treated as the matrimonial home rather than a more inclusive definition of the familial home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to consider expanding its definition to fit in with the times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to have the courage to change the social infrastructure to meet changing social structures and economic circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is a beautiful saying about motherhood: "Being a mother is like having a piece of your heart running outside of you".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And I would go further to say that such love extends to both parents and, frequently, to our extended family as well.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our society recognises the value of these bonds through our policies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The CDCA Bill is a solid step to further support parenthood in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Our parents welcome the additional maternity leave, for it affords them more precious moments with their new-born child.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Both our unwed mothers and adoptive parents also welcome the increase in maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together, it signifies a further step in making our society inclusive and it also signifies that every Singaporean child is precious.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, there is much to celebrate with the passage of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, I would like to speak about two other groups which can benefit more from support.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, foster parents, especially those who are related to the children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, adoptive parents who have tried unsuccessfully to have children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Taken together, families from these two groups may not be large.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But they, too, are part of this society, and the children from these families, too, are precious.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Historically, foster and adoptive parenthood has been well-accepted in our society, especially in post-war Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: While this number has diminished in our society, many of us know elderly relatives who have been fostered or adopted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Foster and adoptive parenthood is, therefore, an accepted part of our societal fabric.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I, therefore, believe we can do more to strengthen support in these areas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, there is still some way to go in Page: 57 achieving MSF's goal.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The existing MSF criteria are: one, resident of Singapore, at least 25 years; two, medically fit to care for children; three, household income of at least $2,000 a month; four, preferably married couples; and five, preferably experienced in caring and living with children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that there is also a monthly allowance per foster child, with more support for a child with special needs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To strengthen foster parenting in Singapore, I hope that the Government can provide foster parents with similar rights as adoptive parents with regard to leave.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, I hope that foster parents can benefit from childcare and extended childcare leave, adoption leave, shared parenthood leave and unpaid infant-care leave.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Because foster parents have parenting duties, just like other parents, and many of them struggle to do so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, such leave will go some way to help them out.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, to enlarge the pool of foster parents, I hope MSF can relax its income criterion of at least $2,000 per month, especially for relatives, such as grandparents, uncles and aunties.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The logic behind the income criterion is understandable.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, there are retirees who have assets but no income who could provide excellent fostering care.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some of these could be relatives who have a deep love for their foster children.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Also, foster parents could also tap on our society for resources to help our children, for example, MSF's monthly allowance I spoke about, as well as all the various social safety nets that we have strengthened over the years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But, of course, we can also have a safeguard where MSF's assessment and approval are needed to overcome this criterion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I hope that the Government can vest MSF with the power to recommend to the Family Justice Court, when necessary, legal guardianship for a selected group of foster parents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We all know that family dynamics can be complicated in cases where fostering is needed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Sometimes, it would be wise if the foster parents, especially relatives of the foster children, could get legal guardianship.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, it costs six to nine months and $5,000 to $7,000 of legal fees to achieve that, which could be a burden to some foster parents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, if MSF is empowered to recommend legal guardianship as needed, we can cut out unnecessary costs.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to talk about easing the financial burden on adoptive parents.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: There is less adoption than it used to be.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The number of adoption agencies has also gone down by half.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For Singaporeans who embark on the adoption process, it is a costly process.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Well, there are not many children available for adoption locally, as many unwanted pregnancies have resulted in abortions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, many potential adoptive parents have to look at adopting from overseas, especially if they want someone who can fit well into their family circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: However, internationally, many countries are strengthening their adoption guidelines, and understandably so.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I can think of two ways to encourage and strengthen adoption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Even after the recent generous increase in subsidies for IVF in public hospitals, many Singaporean couples who tried Page: 58 unsuccessfully to conceive have to still incur costly and repeated IVF treatment, especially if they do so in a private hospital.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These couples would also have drawn down on their MediSave funds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For example, there is a pair of grandparents from Kebun Baru, whose daughter, a single mother herself, has passed on.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, this pair of grandparents are striving and doing their best to be adoptive parents to their grandson.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They are both in their 60s and 70s.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: They are both struggling to have full-time jobs, so that they can support their grandson who is also their adopted son.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: From what I can see, they have no less love for their grandson than any parents out there.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And then there is a 52-year-old widow in Kebun Baru whom the press affectionately called the Bao Lady.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: She is a hawker supporting three children of her own.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: She also takes in unwed mothers, as well as homeless children of all races.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It also acknowledges the growing role of fathers in smaller nuclear families.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also addresses the perennial concerns of single mothers as it provides needed relief to them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While I fully support the changes to the Bill, I also would like to seek clarifications on the following clauses stated in the Bill.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Many workers, especially lower income workers, may not know this.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the employer were to dismiss a pregnant employee, should the employer be made to inform MOM as a default, instead of having the employee to lodge the complaint with MOM as these leave entitlements are associated with employment?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, can this be done by default?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I know this comes under the purview of MOM, but education awareness can be a joint effort of both Ministries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Some unscrupulous employers may find ways and means to shrug off their responsibilities under the Act and resort to easy ways of termination.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This issue has been raised and addressed in the past.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, with the slowing economy, more can be done to protect the interest of these working mothers and fathers as well as pregnant women.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These issues can be jointly addressed by Page: 59 both Ministries, too.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What is the documentary proof required preventing abuse, that is, inflated claims?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the period be stretched to seven days on a case-to-case basis, based on appeal?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On recovery of payment, the Bill states the Government "may" instead of "shall" recover Government Paid Maternity Leave and Government Paid Maternity Benefit beyond statutory limits.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What would be the circumstances where such payments would not be recovered?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As such payments are classified as civil debts, what are the channels to recover these debts?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the numbers are low, how best can we promote sharing of parental leave between fathers and mothers and realise the importance of joint parenting?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The intention of shared parental leave certainly includes the responsibilities of not only mothers but fathers in raising children.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As a society, there must be a more concerted effort to push for shared parenthood.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Be it a single parent or dual-parent family nucleus, the Government has shown, that at the end of it all, it is the child's interest that is of paramount importance and that no child should be deprived, penalised or robbed of parental love through no fault of theirs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The various leave schemes for both natural and adoptive parents are a welcome one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More needs to be done to help young fathers overcome mindset and workplace constraints to improve this consumption rate.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides enhancing leave schemes for young parents, the Government should consider caregivers of elderly and other dependants as well.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It is suggested that we allow flexing of medical leave provided under the Employment Act for caregiving needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I have four points to make on unwed fathers, maternity protection, stay-at-home moms and foster parents.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Enhancements have been made to grant fathers of adoptive children two weeks of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While they may be few but, due to circumstances, there may be fathers who have to bear the responsibility of caring for the infant in the absence of the baby's mother.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Female employees who are pregnant or on maternity leave are protected by law from being dismissed or retrenched.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The transition back to work after maternity leave ends is not an easy period as they learn to cope with balancing demands of work and the needs of their babies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While they were away, their jobs may have been reallocated by employers and, upon their return, these mothers may face possibilities of re-deployment or even redundancy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As a result, these mothers may eventually be out of the workforce, whether by choice or not, and it becomes a lose-lose situation for both the mothers and our economy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The International Labour Organization Maternity Protection Convention No 183 states that, "The standard also prohibits employers to terminate the employment of a woman during pregnancy or absence on maternity leave, or during a period following her return to work, except on grounds unrelated to pregnancy, childbirth and its consequences, or nursing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Women returning to work must be returned to the same position or an equivalent position paid at the same rate." Third, stay-at-home mothers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Studies have shown that women choose to leave the workforce mainly due to family commitments and whether they are raising children or caring for elderly dependants, their contribution is invaluable to our society and nation's development.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: However, the work that these women are doing goes unpaid and they are relying on financial resources of their spouses and loved ones alone.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Without financial independence, their retirement adequacy is questionable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Hence, it should be a priority to provide support and interventions to help these women in securing their retirement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As the educational standards of the workforce rise and women choose to have children later, more and more who leave the workforce are PMEs in mid-career.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This loss to the talent pool can be mitigated by enabling seamless transition of these women back to work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While many of their skills may have become outdated or irrelevant in the many years when they were at home, these PME women do possess skills and experience which can be transferable to new jobs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Various Professional Conversion Programmes (PCPs) targeted at mid-career PMEs can be enhanced to make the jobs more attractive to back-to-work PMEs, the women especially, in terms of pay, career prospects and flexibility in work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the same time, improving on the delivery mode for training and duration will entice more to make the commitment to embark on the PCP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: During the returnship period, women jobseekers are given guidance and training to update their skills, better understand the job and ascertain her suitability for the position.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Upon successful completion of returnship, women jobseekers can embark on PCP for further training to make the career switch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This can all be done through an enhancement of the current CSP and PCP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Besides granting CPF Cash Top Up Relief to encourage spouses and loved ones to voluntarily contribute to the CPF accounts of these stay-at-home moms, the Government should recognise the value of the unpaid work done by these women.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can the Government also regularly top up the accounts of these mothers directly?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the Workfare Scheme, can mothers who are younger than 35 years old and a spouse having a higher than $70,000 assessable income who engage in part-time, temporary or freelance jobs be entitled to cash supplement, CPF contributions and training grants, too?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is to encourage mothers to stay connected with the job market and keep their skills updated while they are away, thus making an entire transition back to the workforce in future a much easier and Page: 61 smoother one.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Expansion of leave to single parents and adoptive parents is laudable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, it is timely to also consider extension of childcare leave to foster parents fostering young children so that they can spend time helping the foster children to settle into their new home.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The Fostering Scheme under MSF provides care arrangements for children who have been abandoned, neglected or ill-treated by their parents or guardians, or those whose parents or guardians are in ill-health and, therefore, unable to look after them.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Some of the amendments have made the definition of parenting more inclusive and give flexibility to accommodate different parenting styles, particularly in the areas of adoption and unwed parents, and provide clarity on administrative matters related to parental entitlements.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The Bill shows that we have positively progressed on some topics where there is a growing trend and our willingness to recognise and accept some diversity in family nucleus.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I remember a few striking cases of my own residents who attempted to have their own children but they were unable to due to age and also medical conditions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The tremendous efforts these families undertook to adopt the children from overseas impressed upon me that it is not the financial aids that we provide that are material to them, but the acknowledgement from society that they are akin to the child's natural parents for their love in raising the child as though it is their own and also the fairness in including them under such benefit schemes that really makes the difference.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Similarly, for cases where marital status used to be the qualifying criterion, with the introduction of the new amendments, this would help quite a number of families with differing circumstances.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: As I believe Child Development Account (CDA) touches the lives of every child and family in Singapore, the schemes implemented therein should not only encourage the families to have more children, but to give those children who are from vulnerable background a boost and also a better quality in life.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Today, the CDA fund is given to every child at birth and can be utilised when it is used at the approved institutions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, I feel that the low-income families may not be able to benefit fully from this scheme.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Thirdly, some families with challenging backgrounds are using this pretext of lack of funds to delay enrolling their children for pre-school or childcare.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Page: 62 First, to assist parents who are already receiving the aids from the Social Service Office or those with low-income capped at specific limits and who have young children and school-going children in maximising the usage of the CDA funds.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Third, to facilitate our public donors who wish to contribute funds to these low-income families by topping up the CDAs of the needy in order for the savings to receive these matching grants.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: And fourth, to permit the parents or even trustees to tap on the CDA funds to purchase education endowment or insurance policies for these children.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Through some of all these above suggestions, we can better support those children in need and enable social and financial support to be given by willing individuals, apart from the child's natural parents or even legal guardians.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This also extends the aid beyond the early childhood and Primary schooling years of the children and better utilise the funds provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is about the time we have with them, it is about the time we spend with them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I fully and wholeheartedly applaud MSF for the amendments they are proposing in this Bill and for levelling the playing field for fathers, for adoptive parents and for single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These amendments move us one huge step forward towards becoming a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parenthood has been one of the greatest joys in my life and it remains close to my heart to see that every parent in Singapore is able to watch their child speak their first words, walk their first steps and hold their hand every step of the way.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ample research has shown that the bonds forged between parent and child in the earlier stage of his or her development is a one-time opportunity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thus, this remains one of my highest priorities: contributing my thoughts and suggestions about parenthood.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These changes send a strong signal of the Government's resolve to put family first.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is reflective of a Government policy which keeps up with the times as adoption becomes more common.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I applaud these changes, I would like to ask the Minister why adoptive parents are not given the same benefits as birth parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why does adoption leave only apply to children under 12 months old?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why do adoptive mothers who qualify for leave still get only 12 weeks of maternity leave compared to the full 18 weeks?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that adoptive mothers do not require extra time to recuperate after childbirth, but it is still important to note that adoptive mothers – like birth mothers – require time to bond with their babies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Could we further consider the age of the child to determine the length of parental leave accorded to adoptive parents, and consider giving adoptive mothers the full 18 weeks of maternity leave if they have adopted a new-born or a baby under a certain age?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hear about the struggles they face, the risks they are exposed to.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, can the Minister share what are the factors delaying the complete levelling of this playing field?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, Madam, I spoke at the Second Reading of the Child Development Co-Savings Bill in May this year and I spoke about my wish to have the power to turn back time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In that speech, I said, "As much as I try to live a life without regret, there will always be regrets, always a wish that we could have done things better, always a wish that we could have spent more time with our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Time spent with our children is precious and should be cherished, the memories created will last forever and are priceless.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can't buy time and we can't turn back time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can't get back the hours, the minutes and the seconds lost.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we can every day treasure and value the time we have with our children and our loved ones." I did not mention this earlier but when I wrote that speech and, in particular, those few paragraphs, I was thinking about my late father who passed away last year and whom I miss dearly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He worked hard but he did not work hard for himself or purely for money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He never wore branded clothes or liked expensive things.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But he worked hard for his family, his company and his staff members.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He never really had time for family and he passed on before he retired, before he was about to have more time for family, especially his grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is a quote, which reads, "Spend time with those you love.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of these days you will either reply, "I'm glad I did," or "I wish I had"." For my father, I am sure his reply was: "I wish I had" and, with him, I wish I had, too, but I know that I cannot turn back time and I will have to live with that regret.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for my children, I will make sure my reply is "I'm glad I did" and I hope everyone will ask yourselves this question as you embark on your parenthood journey and even those already on Page: 64 this journey.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I mentioned in my previous speeches that this journey has changed me and it continues to change me.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My daughter remains the most stubborn person in my family, she continues to say "no" all the time, even though it is actually more "nos" now – to be exact, it is five "nos" at a go: "no, no, no, no, no".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Her favourite words are now: "Daddy, what is this?" or "Daddy, what is that?" I swear she even says this in her sleep.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thankfully, for parents these days, there is something called "Google"!

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But there was a one-for-one offer and so I am happy to announce we are also expecting our third child – we are having twins!

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just saying the word "twins" makes me feel tired already but we are extremely excited about welcoming our two little girls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I look forward to welcoming them into this world and to spending time with them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I have to say that after these two little girls, this factory is closed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As a father of a young daughter, it is perhaps only appropriate that I declare my interest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But unlike my fellow Member Mr Louis Ng, I do not have good news to update.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill is very timely, especially during a time when our young mothers and fathers face tremendous constraints in managing work and family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two important messages in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, families need greater support and we can help fathers to play a larger role in caring for their children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Two, every Singaporean child is important and must be given every chance to fulfil his or her potential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As my fellow Labour Member of Parliament, Mr Zainal Sapari, often reminds us, the younger Members of Parliament – he is a wonderful father to six lovely children, so he has every right to do so – that to be in your children's memories tomorrow, you have to be in their lives today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This Bill does include support and provision and time for parents to rightfully fulfil what he has advised us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is trite knowledge that our younger Singaporeans are finding it increasingly difficult to raise a family and have a meaningful career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, gender stereotypes on child-caring is evolving.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is already archaic to think that only women Page: 65 must bear the primary care-giving role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fathers play an important role in a child's life, especially in the early years, with substantial downstream social and cognitive benefits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The proposed provisions are also in line with an evolving change in gender-based family stereotypes and redefinition of traditional roles at home.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I am glad for these provisions, I am cautious for the eventual consumption of the additional week of paternity leave or shared parental leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This shows that our families might face structural problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Common anecdotally-evidenced gaps include the lack of support from employers, especially smaller companies which might genuinely face operational constraints.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Fathers with reservist duties are also hesitant to take leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, some employers have commented it is difficult to support two types of national service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Both employers and employees need help for this to be effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I still maintain that it is only right that we send a strong signal of support through legislation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we will need to study its implementation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   : Mdm Speaker, I fully agree that we should legislate to give fathers an additional week of paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Nowadays, more and more young Singaporeans believe that both parents should be involved in taking care of the children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The traditional concept of mothers being the primary caregiver of children is also changing gradually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, during the first year of a newborn, the mother still plays the primary role.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, we need to help mothers ease the dual responsibilities of caring for her child as well as managing her career.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This additional week of paternity leave will help fathers to play a more active role in taking care of the children and help reduce the burden on the mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For first-time fathers, this is indeed timely by giving them the opportunity to lay a solid foundation for an ideal family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This measure also reflects Singaporeans' changing mindset with regard to what a good marriage and family should be like.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, we cannot just legislate without considering the effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The take-up rate of paternity leave is still very low.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I urge the Government to encourage more businesses to support their staff utilising paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We do acknowledge the value of a traditional family structure of a married couple with children.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, in reality, not all families come in the same form or structure.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And he or she deserves every chance at a full life and fulfilling his or her potential.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, I support the extension of CDA to children born to unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a big move towards greater inclusiveness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It will promote savings and help their mothers defray the cost of childcare or other needs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Page: 66 Madam, while these measures have narrowed the gap between the entitlements of what a married woman with a child would get and that of an unwed mother, there are still areas where unwed mothers are not extended the same treatment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Government consider extending this to them, in full or in part, as this will go a long way in helping unwed mothers cope with the costs of raising a child, especially when they have to do so without the support of a spouse?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I also urge the Government to extend the following tax reliefs to unwed mothers: Working Mother's Child Relief, Grandparent Care-giver Relief, Foreign Maid Levy Relief and the Parenthood Tax Rebate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is because the money saved could go towards the needs of the child and, if we are to fully embrace the mantra "Every Child Matters", then we should treat them equally by not denying their parents access to these reliefs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This means they have to rent a place if they are not able to live with their family or relatives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sometimes, family members are not able to accommodate them due to space constraints.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: To recap, the key amendments are based on enhancements which were announced earlier at my Ministry's and NPTD's Committee of Supply debates in April this year.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am glad that Members, such as Mr Alex Yam, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Seah Kian Peng, Miss Cheryl Chan, Mr Desmond Choo, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh and Ms Thanaletchimi, support the extension of maternity leave benefits to unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These will improve the outcomes of their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Assoc Prof Goh shared his concern about housing security for children of unwed parents and divorcees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He asked if the Government could include unwed parents in its definition of family nucleus in assessing applications for HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Seah, Mr Alex Yam and Mr Choo asked if housing options can be improved for this group, such as allowing unwed mothers to purchase an HDB flat before turning 35.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Our public housing policy recognises the traditional family unit.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That said, single unwed parents are not without housing options.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Those aged 35 and above may apply for a new 2-room flexi flat in a non-mature estate or a resale flat and also enjoy housing grants.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Those below 35 Page: 67 years old may apply for new HDB flats or resale flats jointly with their parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As for divorced parents with young children, they are given priority under HDB's assistance scheme for second-timers when they apply for a new 2- or 3-room BTO flat in non-mature estates.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Additionally, on a case-by-case basis, HDB also exercises flexibility to help divorced parents and single unwed parents buy a flat within their means, or to provide rental housing to those with no other housing options or family support.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether unwed fathers could be granted paternity leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is generally the case that unwed mothers would be the main care-givers of their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, we will consider appeals by unwed fathers on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: All working parents, regardless of marital status, can avail themselves to infant care and childcare leave to meet their care-giving needs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Louis Ng, Mr Alex Yam, Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Desmond Choo asked if more could be done for unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Some suggestions include the extension of Baby Bonus Cash Gift and tax benefits.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is good to take stock of the support we have given to all Singapore children to enhance child outcomes, regardless of whether their parents are married.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I have said this a couple of times in this House and I think it is important for me to repeat it here again.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: These are education and healthcare benefits and they include the MediSave grant for newborns, and infant and childcare subsidies.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: All working parents, regardless of marital status, also get infant care leave, childcare leave and extended childcare leave and the Foreign Domestic Worker levy concession to support caregiving to enhance child outcomes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think many Members' concerns centre around children who come from more vulnerable backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If you compound that with unwed parents, it makes it even more difficult for them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We know that children of unwed parents from low-income and vulnerable families need even more support, which is why we are introducing KidSTART.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It may be in its pilot stage but we hope and want this to work, so that we can extend this much more extensively amongst the vulnerable families, even starting from Year Zero when women can be identified at the pregnancy stage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Financial and social support is also available at Social Service Offices and Family Service Centres.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I urge Members to take note that, even for unwed mothers, there is a range of support available.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: With the recent changes and the changes we are putting in place, it extends it further.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, it is also important to understand that we continue to believe in the importance of the family institution.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Hence, specific measures, for example, the Baby Bonus Cash Gift, tax benefits and Government co-funding for Assisted Reproduction Technology treatment and priority for housing, are targeted at married families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: However, as mentioned earlier, for unwed parents, there are also ways in which we can support them through various schemes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Ng also asked whether adoption leave could be extended to adoptive mothers of children older than 12 months.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Similar to maternity and paternity leave, adoption leave is intended to support parents of infants in the first year of delivery.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Beyond the child's infancy, all working parents – including adoptive parents – can take six days each of paid childcare leave when the child Page: 68 is below age seven, and six more days of unpaid infant care leave when the child is below age two, to spend more time to bond with their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Henry Kwek touched on the need for our society to support adoption.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He suggested a grant to offset foreign adoption costs for couples who have failed repeatedly to conceive.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As the focus of adoption is to find a suitable family for a child, subsidising the fees charged by commercial adoption agencies is not the right solution in terms of protecting the best interests of the child.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Kwek also suggested allowing single parents who were previously married and have adopted a related child to benefit from the Parenthood Tax Rebate.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We thank him for the suggestion, which we will study further.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That said, all things being equal and in the child's best interest, we encourage parenthood within marriage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That is still something that we would like to see and encourage.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Members, including Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Kwek, also raised suggestions to support foster parents, through various measures, such as leave benefits.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, I visited her and spoke to her and her family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is quite encouraging to see families with such capacity to love, not just for their children but for many children over many years.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It really makes a difference to these children whose families may not be ready to take them in and look after them for a period.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are heartened to see that Singaporeans are willing to go that extra mile to care for vulnerable children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We certainly want to encourage more Singaporeans to come on board to be foster parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will keep the suggestions in mind as we continue to develop foster care.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I will now move on to the topic of stay-at-home mothers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked if the Government would consider putting in place Returnship Programmes to help match women jobseekers and employers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He also suggested providing an Income Supplement to stay-at-home mothers and for Workfare Scheme benefits to be extended to a select group of such young mothers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I think this is an idea that we can consider, though we should take a hard look at all the current job-matching services and to minimise duplication of efforts.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But I think this is something that we should work at.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I want to assure Members that we recognise and value the contributions of stay-at-home mothers in caring for their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We appreciate the suggestions from Members and will take them into consideration as we continue to study ways to enhance the family-friendly environment in Singapore, to support both working and non-working parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Patrick Tay is right that there are other caregivers, such as those of the elderly and other dependants.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: He suggested allowing flexing of medical leave under the Employment Act with them, as they may not qualify for the current leave benefits.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While we want to support such caregivers, we also need to consider the impact on businesses and the overall leave support already in place for employees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Tay asked to extend protection beyond pregnancy and maternity leave for female employees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will work with tripartite partners in the next round of review to study this, while being mindful not to change the laws so drastically that it results in unintended consequences, Page: 69 such as resentment against mothers and impact on gender bias because this could impact on their employability.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something that we have to be careful about.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Nonetheless, it is an important area to look at.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In the meantime, we will continue to encourage employers to adopt flexible work arrangements to support families.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh highlighted the need to protect contract workers as this group is fast becoming a substantial group in the gig economy.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In fact, when I was in MOM, this was an area that we flagged out for close attention.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: But we also realised that this whole space is quite complex because there are many, many different types of contract work.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: MOM will work with our tripartite partners to study this suggestion further, taking into consideration the overall leave provisions already in place by employers and the care-giving needs of workers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Thanaletchimi raised four technical areas for clarification under this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: MOM encourages employers to implement fair and non-discriminatory employment practices.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TAFEP) takes an active role in looking into complaints of unfair employment practices and will refer cases to MOM for enforcement if found to be true.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Any employee who feels discriminated against can approach TAFEP for assistance.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will determine the amount of Government-Paid Maternity Benefit for such a woman based on documents, such as her payslip.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where there is reason to doubt the documents or the claims, we will ask further questions and may not always approve the claim.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Thirdly, she asked how the weekly index works for a person who works seven days a week.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The weekly index simplifies the provisions of the Act and does not change entitlement.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Where maternity leave is taken flexibly, it will be based on the number of days she works in a week, or 48 days, whichever is lower.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This mirrors the computation of entitlement for employees on continuous and non-continuous leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Fourthly, she asked about the circumstances and mechanism under which the Government will recover over-payment of Government-Paid Maternity Leave and Government-Paid Maternity Benefit.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: As with other civil debts, the Government has the option to commence legal proceedings to recover over-payment of Government-Paid Maternity Leave and Government-Paid Maternity Benefit.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In practice, we will seek to recover through calls, letters or physical visits if necessary.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Ms Thanaletchimi said that employees whose services are terminated with just cause cease to be entitled to Adoptive Leave, Government-Paid Maternity Leave and Government-Paid Paternity Leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: If she had worked satisfactorily in other jobs in the 12 months preceding delivery, she can still receive a Government-Paid Maternity Benefit amount based on income earned from those jobs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Miss Cheryl Chan suggested some enhancements relating to CDAs.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Miss Chan would be pleased to hear CDA monies can be used to purchase the child's premiums for MediShield Life or MediSave-approved plans.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: At the end of 12 years, unused CDA monies are also automatically transferred to the child's Post-Secondary Education Account which can be used for post-Secondary Page: 70 education fees.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: She also suggested that the Government facilitate donors or payments of cash assistance into the CDAs of children from low-income families, so that they can benefit more from the CDA scheme.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is directly provided into newly opened CDAs, without parents having to save first.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also reach out to lower income families through touchpoints, such as the Social Service Offices and Family Service Centres, to increase awareness about the CDA.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We also welcome initiatives by society to help families defray the cost of child-raising.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One such example is the OCBC Starter Scheme, which was introduced in 2012 and will end in December 2016.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On Mr Louis Ng's request for the updated take-up rates for Paternity Leave, this was 38% in 2014 and 42% in 2015; an improvement of 4%.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is not bad, but we hope this will increase further.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The 2015 figure is still increasing and will only be finalised at the end of March 2017, when the deadline for the submission of claims is over.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: On Ms Thanaletchimi's request for statistics, about 4,000 fathers have taken shared parental leave as at the end of August 2016.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng asked if independent leave can be considered.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are now increasing paternity leave and shared parental leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: For any further leave enhancements, we need to balance the needs and concerns of both employees and employers.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We will also look into Mr Desmond Choo's suggestion for an in-depth study of constraints faced by companies and fathers in consuming these two leave schemes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The enhancements to paternity leave and shared parental leave signal the Government's strong support to encourage fathers to spend more time caring for their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Shared parental leave also provides parents the flexibility to decide and to choose their leave arrangements to care for their newborns, based on their respective family's circumstances.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We really hope that more fathers will make use of the enhanced leave to be involved in child-raising.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: That being said, ultimately, it is for the father to decide whether to take the leave or not.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Maybe we should persuade mothers to convince fathers to take the leave.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: And I encourage Mr Desmond Choo to work harder.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I also thank Mr Louis Ng for his interesting parenting experiences.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I am sure many of us who are parents here will have our respective interesting stories as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Indeed, those of us who can look back and honestly say, "I am glad I did", remember the lessons we learnt as parents.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Children enrich our lives in the most unexpected ways, just as we fathers play an important role in the family.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We are not just breadwinners, but we are role models for our children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: We really need to be active and present in our children's lives, especially during our child's formative years.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In MSF, when we look at the various social issues, there are two common denominators that we pick up, as we connect the dots and trace it back.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: A lot has got to do with a stable family Page: 71 environment and, especially, the presence of the father.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The other point is about making an impact in the formative years, where the greatest development is experienced by our child.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Mothers are usually there, but fathers need to be there as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: This is something that we can encourage and support but, ultimately, the individual parents must make those choices.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Fathers can shape a child's confidence immensely in their development.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I fully agree with Mr Seah Kian Peng's point that, as parents, we should be focusing on the child's health, growth and well-being.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Parents sometimes do not know what impact their comparisons have on their children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: In some situations, the child loses confidence in his ability and he starts to wonder if he will be unloved by his parents the moment he fails to meet their expectations.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Fathers have the means to demonstrate unconditional love and support to the children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I urge all of us to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: While this will certainly help working parents, more and more young fathers are willing to make use of these facilities and not just expect the mothers to do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Families for Life as well as Government agencies provide parenting and family events and workshops at the workplaces.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I encourage more fathers to avail themselves of these and to be more engaged in pro-family workplace programmes.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: One important tagline says, we are "Dads for Life".

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: I hope that we, as fathers, will continue to be involved and always present in our children's lives.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It may be different for everyone, and we all need to find our own way to connect and bond with our children.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It could be through simple everyday activities like reading a bedtime story, kicking a soccer ball around, going out to cycle or just going out for a meal.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It may surprise some of us but, to our children, it is not what we do, but that we are doing it together with them.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: Fathers show that they care and are committed to their wives and their families when they share the parenthood journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: The journey may be a bumpy ride with ups and downs, but we learn along the way to be better parents ‒ together with our spouses.

speaker: Mr Tan Chuan-Jin
text: It is also these ups and downs that result in the creation of special moments and memories, memories unique to our families, memories which we will always hold dear to ourselves and memories which will last us a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Indeed, we all want to make sure that the two-week mandated paternity leave will be fully taken up.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: But I think Page: 72 if we do not address the source, we are not going to get there.
